title: IP Geolocation Lookup: Accuracy, Privacy, and Where Requests Go
description: IP geolocation: parsing stays local, geolocation goes only to same-origin /api/ip, domains resolve via Ali/Cloudflare DoH. Accuracy, privacy and failure paths.
content:
Looking up IP geolocation means entering an address and reading the “Geolocation Info” panel; but first separate two ideas: geolocation is the registration and data-center geography of an IP, not the location of a device. This page keeps address parsing in the browser; only geolocation and domain resolution go online.

1. The short version: one lookup in three stages

The site's IP address lookup splits a query into three stages. The first is local parsing: IPv4/IPv6 syntax, address class, base conversion and subnet calculation all happen in the browser with no network request. The second is geolocation: after you enter a valid address, the page waits about 900 ms and then sends a same-origin request to /api/ip?ip=…, or you can click “Resolve and Lookup” to query immediately. The third is domains: when you type something like example.com, the page first turns the domain into an IP through DNS-over-HTTPS, then runs local parsing and the online geolocation lookup on the first IP.

The three stages map to three panels: “My IP” shows the current network egress, “IP Address Lookup” shows the local computation, and “Geolocation Info” shows the online result. The point is not to memorize the city for a given IP but to know where each number comes from, where each request goes, and which fields can be empty.

2. What has already happened when the page opens

The last line of the page script is void refreshSelf(): on load it immediately requests the same-origin /api/ip and fills both “My IP” and the geolocation panel. Open the page without typing anything and there has already been one request with no parameters, returning the visitor's own egress IP and the Cloudflare edge geography.

The initial hint in “IP Address Lookup” is “Enter an IP or domain to resolve it automatically (computed locally, no network required)”. It describes the parsing panel only and does not cover the geolocation query; the geolocation empty state has its own wording, “After lookup, country, ISP, coordinates and other geolocation details are shown (online lookup)”.

“Sample” cycles through 9 samples in a fixed order and queries each immediately; “Clear” empties the input and hides the parsing and geolocation panels, but leaves the “My IP” panel alone (it keeps the egress IP from the last lookup) and does not change the URL or write history; “Paste” reads the clipboard and queries at once. The subnet prefix dropdown appears only for IPv4.

3. Local parsing: syntax first, then bases

IPv4 parsing requires four octets, each 1–3 digits and 0–255, and rejects leading zeros outright with /^0\d/: 010.0.0.1 is not treated as IPv4. IPv6 first handles an embedded IPv4 (such as ::ffff:8.8.8.8), then pads :: out to 8 groups and validates each group as 1–4 hex digits. Once validation passes, the page shows decimal, hexadecimal, binary and the ::ffff: mapping for IPv4; for IPv6 it shows the expanded form, the compressed form and the embedded IPv4.

  • 8.8.8.8 → decimal 134744072, hexadecimal 0x08080808, binary 00001000.00001000.00001000.00001000, mapped ::ffff:8.8.8.8.
  • 2001:4860:4860::8888 → expands to 2001:4860:4860:0000:0000:0000:0000:8888, compresses back to 2001:4860:4860::8888.
  • ::ffff:8.8.8.8 → expands to 0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:ffff:0808:0808, compresses to ::ffff:808:808, with a separate line for the embedded IPv4 8.8.8.8.

Compression folds the longest run of consecutive zeros, and only runs at least 2 long. So ::ffff:8.8.8.8 compresses to ::ffff:808:808, not the familiar dotted form; the page also does not turn the last 32 bits back into dotted decimal.

4. Classification badges: order decides which rule hits

IPv4 classification is an interval table walked in order: V4_RANGES has 15 entries, from 0.0.0.0/8 to 240.0.0.0/4, each with a length, a label and an RFC. The first match returns, so the table's order is its priority; 255.255.255.255 is checked separately before the walk as “limited broadcast”, and a public address that matches no row falls through to “Public IPv4 (0.0.0.0/0)”.

InputBadgeDefault subnet
192.168.1.100Private address (192.168.0.0/16)/16
10.1.1.1Private address (10.0.0.0/8)/8
100.64.0.1Carrier-grade NAT (100.64.0.0/10)/10
127.0.0.1Loopback address (127.0.0.0/8)/8
169.254.1.1Link-local (169.254.0.0/16)/16
224.0.0.1Multicast address (224.0.0.0/4)/4
240.0.0.1Reserved address (240.0.0.0/4)/4
255.255.255.255Limited broadcast (255.255.255.255)/32
192.0.2.1Documentation example (192.0.2.0/24)/24
198.51.100.7Documentation example (198.51.100.0/24)/24
203.0.113.9Documentation example (203.0.113.0/24)/24
198.18.0.1Benchmark testing (198.18.0.0/15)/15
8.8.8.8Public IPv4/24

The default subnet follows the classification: when a row matches, its length is used, and only public IPv4 has no length of its own, so it defaults to /24. Hence 10.1.1.1 offers only /8, 100.64.0.1 only /10, 192.168.1.100 only /16; only public addresses get the seven options /8 /16 /24 /28 /30 /31 /32.

The IPv6 table has 11 entries, covering unspecified, loopback, IPv4-mapped, NAT64, documentation example, IETF protocol assignment, deprecated address, 6to4, unique local, link-local and multicast. IPv6 shows no subnet panel: when the version is 6 the page hides “Subnet Info” outright, and although the default prefix field is written as 64 it has no rendered entry point.

5. Subnet math: /31 and /32 do not subtract two

The subnet computes the network address with a bitwise AND and the broadcast address with a bitwise OR; the address count is 2 to the power of (32 minus the prefix). Usable addresses are the total minus 2 at /30 and shorter prefixes (dropping the network and broadcast addresses); at /31 and /32 nothing is subtracted: both addresses are usable at /31, and /32 has exactly 1. That branch is written usable = prefix >= 31 ? total : total - 2.

Address and prefixSubnet CIDRBroadcast addressAddress count
8.8.8.8 /248.8.8.0/248.8.8.255Total 256, usable 254
8.8.8.8 /318.8.8.8/318.8.8.92 usable
8.8.8.8 /328.8.8.8/328.8.8.81 usable
10.1.1.1 /810.0.0.0/810.255.255.255Total 16,777,216, usable 16,777,214

Note the /31 row: 8.8.8.8 is even, so its /31 is 8.8.8.8/31 with broadcast address 8.8.8.9, not 8.8.8.0/31. The subnet is computed from the address you enter, not from the start of its class block.

6. The geolocation request: the browser only calls same-origin /api/ip

In the current version of this page the online geolocation request goes only to the same-origin /api/ip. Without parameters the function returns the visitor's IP and the Cloudflare edge geography fields, with the response header Cache-Control: no-store; with ?ip= the function acts as a proxy: IPv4 is forwarded to https://ipapi.co/<ip>/json/ and IPv6 to https://ipwho.is/<ip>, normalized into one set of fields, with the UA fixed at CloverTools-IP-Lookup/1.0 and the response header public, max-age=3600. The browser never contacts ipapi.co or ipwho.is directly.

ActionBrowser requestActual destinationCache header
Open the pageGET /api/ipCloudflare edge (request.cf)no-store
Enter a valid IPGET /api/ip?ip=…Cloudflare Function, then ipapi.co or ipwho.ispublic, max-age=3600
Enter a domain, A recordGET dns.alidns.com/resolve?name=…&type=1Alibaba Public DNS; Cloudflare if there is no answerSet by the third party
Enter a domain, AAAA recordGET dns.alidns.com/resolve?name=…&type=28Alibaba Public DNS; Cloudflare if there is no answerSet by the third party

A valid IP does not trigger a request immediately: the page waits 250 ms for debounce, then another 900 ms to confirm the input has not changed, before calling doOnline(); clicking “Resolve and Lookup” or pressing Enter queries at once. Domain resolution skips the 900 ms: once a domain is detected the page calls resolveDomain(), asks AliDNS first and Cloudflare when there is no answer, in the type order A (1) then AAAA (28), and the first answer wins.

The bottom of the geolocation panel always reads “Data source: Cloudflare Edge”, because both paths pass cloudflare as the source; although SOURCE_NAME has ipapi and ipwhois keys, the code never uses them. On the ?ip= path the data actually comes from ipapi.co or ipwho.is, yet the footer still says Cloudflare Edge.

The proxy path has two more formatting differences: ipapi normalization takes the upstream asn: "AS15169" and prepends another AS, producing ASAS15169; and the UTC offset field names do not line up — the function outputs the key utcOffset, while the front end reads only raw.utc_offset or raw.offset, so the time zone row shows only America/Los_Angeles and never (UTC-0800). On the parameterless path both country and countryCode come from request.cf.country, so the Country/Region row shows “US (US)”.

Measured on the day (around 2026-11-10T22:00Z): the parameterless GET /api/ip returned 200 JSON; ?ip=8.8.8.8, ?ip=2001:4860:4860::8888 and ?ip=.. all returned HTTP 502 Cloudflare error pages rather than the JSON error body from the function's catch. This was the edge's behavior that day and does not mean the path always fails.

7. Accuracy limits: registered geography is not device location

Geolocation comes from the registration information and data-center location in an IP database, usually accurate to country, province/state and city, sometimes with postal code and coordinates, but it is not GPS or Wi-Fi positioning. Roaming across cities, corporate leased lines and cloud hosts all make “where the IP is” differ from “where the person is”.

  • Private, loopback, link-local, documentation, multicast and reserved addresses have no global geolocation; the page still calls the online API, but these addresses are outside global registration, so an online lookup is meaningless for them and the result may be empty or fail.
  • Behind CGNAT (100.64.0.0/10) and carrier NAT, many users share an egress IP, so geolocation reaches the carrier or city at best and cannot identify a person.
  • Coordinates can be missing. In the parameterless response measured that day, latitude and longitude were both null, and the page shows the “Coordinates” row and the “View on map” link only when both are numbers.
  • The time zone field comes from the IP database (for example America/Los_Angeles), not from the browser's local time zone; it is a clue, not evidence of the device's time zone.

One more limit comes from the input itself. IPv4 leading zeros are rejected by the local parser, but 010.0.0.1 still passes the page's domain regex, so it is sent to DoH as a domain: the automatic path shows “Domain resolution failed”, and a manual query shows “Unable to resolve 010.0.0.1”. The message “Unrecognized: please enter a valid IP address (IPv4/IPv6) or domain name” appears only for input that fails even the domain regex, such as 1.2.3. or abc.

8. Privacy: what traffic the visit, the input and the domain each create

Separate “computed locally” from “looked up online” and the privacy boundary becomes clear. Opening the page requests the same-origin /api/ip; entering a valid IP sends a same-origin /api/ip?ip=… request after about 900 ms. Both target this site's API, but the function also contacts ipapi.co or ipwho.is on the server, so “the browser did not contact a third party” does not mean “the third party never received this IP”.

Domain resolution is a separate path: the browser sends the domain you typed to dns.alidns.com, then to cloudflare-dns.com if that fails or has no answer, so the domain appears in a third party's DNS requests. The page has no “turn off automatic lookup” switch, and no history list or local storage; request headers and server logs are outside the page code's control.

  • To do local parsing only and avoid the geolocation request, there is currently no interface switch; you can clear the input immediately after typing, or intercept /api/ip with browser developer tools, but those are external measures.

9. Failure messages and next steps

When the geolocation request fails, the panel first shows “Querying location…” and then the empty state changes to “Location lookup failed. Please check your network connection and try again.”, with the status line “Query failed: all data sources unavailable”. A 502 from the function takes the same branch; the page does not distinguish timeouts, rate limits and edge errors.

“Clear” hides the panel and empties the table, but does not reset the empty-state text: after a failed lookup, clearing leaves the geolocation panel reading “Location lookup failed. Please check your network connection and try again.”, and only a page refresh returns it to the initial hint.

To see the request itself more clearly, pair this page with HTTP API Tester for response headers, User-Agent Parser to check the client identity, URL Parameter Parser to split parameterized addresses, and Base Converter to convert between bases. This article describes the current version of this page and what was measured that day; it is not network-location or privacy-compliance advice.

faqs.q: Can IP geolocation find a specific street or house number?
faqs.a: Usually not. Geolocation is the registration and data-center geography in an IP database, commonly accurate to country, province/state and city, sometimes with postal code and coordinates; it is not GPS or Wi-Fi positioning. Even when different networks in the same city share one registered point, the page can only show that point.

faqs.q: Why does an address such as 192.168.1.100 have no geolocation?
faqs.a: 192.168.0.0/16 is an RFC 1918 private network and has no global registration. The page labels it locally as “Private address (192.168.0.0/16)” and still calls the online API after you type it, but addresses like this are outside global registration, so the result may be empty or show a failed lookup.

faqs.q: Why does 010.0.0.1 say “Unable to resolve” instead of “Unrecognized”?
faqs.a: parseIpv4 rejects leading zeros with /^0\d/, so it is not valid IPv4; but the page then tests the domain regex, 010.0.0.1 passes, and so it is sent to DoH as a domain. On an empty answer the automatic path shows “Domain resolution failed”, while a manual query shows “Unable to resolve 010.0.0.1”. Only input that fails even the domain regex, such as 1.2.3. or abc, shows “Unrecognized: please enter a valid IP address (IPv4/IPv6) or domain name”.

faqs.q: Where do domain queries go, and does the domain get exposed?
faqs.a: The browser first sends the domain to dns.alidns.com, switches to cloudflare-dns.com when the A record has no answer, then queries AAAA in the same order; only when both fail does it report a resolution failure. The domain appears in third-party DNS requests, so do not look up domains containing internal project names or personal information on an untrusted public network.

faqs.q: Does the page keep a query history?
faqs.a: The page code has no history list or local storage; Clear only resets the input and the parsing and geolocation panels, and leaves the “My IP” panel alone. But opening the page requests /api/ip, a valid address automatically requests /api/ip?ip=…, and domains trigger requests to two DoH providers; those requests, server logs and CDN logs are outside the page code's control.

faqs.q: Why does the footer say “Data source: Cloudflare Edge” while the ASN is ASAS15169?
faqs.a: The footer takes a fixed source string, and both the lookup and parameterless paths pass cloudflare; the ?ip= path is actually proxied by the function to ipapi.co or ipwho.is. ASAS15169 appears because the function's ipapi normalization appends another AS to the upstream AS15169; the same proxy path also writes the UTC offset as utcOffset while the front end reads utc_offset and offset, so the field names do not match and the time zone row shows no UTC parenthesis.

focus: IP geolocation tells you the registration and data-center geography of an IP, not the device's location. This page keeps IPv4/IPv6 syntax, classification, base conversion and subnet math in the browser and requests only same-origin /api/ip for geolocation; domains go straight to Alibaba's and Cloudflare's DoH. Only by understanding where each request goes can you read “Data source: Cloudflare Edge”, ASAS15169, missing coordinates and 502 failures correctly.
